title: The Divide-and-Conquer Paradigm

related.label: Recursion

summary: Solving a problem by breaking it into smaller instances of itself, solving each independently, and combining their results — the general pattern recursion already introduced, now studied as a design strategy in its own right.

title: Solving Recurrences
summary: Turning a divide-and-conquer algorithm's self-referential running time — T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n), for example — into a closed-form bound, by recursion trees and pattern-matching against a few canonical shapes.

title: Merge Sort Revisited

related.label: Sorting Algorithms: An Introduction
Mergesort: Guaranteed O(n log n) via Divide and Merge

summary: The same merge sort already met as one option among several — now studied rigorously as the canonical divide-and-conquer algorithm, with its T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) recurrence solved in full.

title: The Comparison-Sort Lower Bound
summary: Why no algorithm that sorts purely by comparing elements can beat O(n log n) in the worst case — a genuine impossibility proof, via a decision-tree argument, not just an unmet goal.

references.label: ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Algorithms and Complexity Knowledge Area

title: Quicksort: Partitioning

related.label: Quicksort: Partitioning, Pivots, and Two Textbook Schemes

summary: A different divide-and-conquer sort — pick a pivot, partition everything smaller to its left and everything larger to its right, then recurse on each side — all done in place, unlike merge sort.

title: Quicksort: Average-Case Analysis and Randomization
summary: Quicksort's worst case is O(n²) on an already-sorted or adversarial input, but choosing the pivot at random makes that worst case astronomically unlikely, giving expected O(n log n) on any input.

title: Quicksort vs. Merge Sort: Choosing a Sort
summary: Both hit the O(n log n) lower bound on average, but for genuinely different reasons and with genuinely different trade-offs — in-place vs. extra memory, stable vs. not, worst-case guarantee vs. expected performance.

title: Searching Beyond Binary Search

related.label: Binary Search: O(log n) Lookup on a Sorted Array

summary: Binary search's divide-and-conquer idea generalizes past a plain sorted array — searching a rotated sorted array in O(log n) is a genuinely different, worth-solving puzzle built on the exact same pattern.

references.label: ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Algorithms and Complexity Knowledge Area

title: The Greedy Paradigm

related.label: Greedy Algorithms: Activity Selection and Why the Right Greedy Choice Matters

summary: Building a solution by always taking the locally best-looking choice and never reconsidering it — a strategy that is sometimes provably optimal and sometimes simply wrong, with no way to tell which without a proof.

references.label: ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Algorithms and Complexity Knowledge Area

title: Proving Greedy Optimality: Activity Selection
summary: Scheduling the maximum number of non-overlapping activities by always picking the one that finishes earliest — and a full exchange-argument proof that this greedy choice never costs you the optimal solution.

references.label: ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Algorithms and Complexity Knowledge Area

title: Breadth-First Search

related.label: Graphs: Terminology and Representations
Breadth-First Search

summary: Exploring a graph level by level with a queue, from a chosen source — the algorithm that finds shortest paths, measured in number of edges, in any unweighted graph.

title: Connected Components via BFS
summary: Running BFS from every not-yet-visited vertex partitions an undirected graph into its connected components — a direct, practical payoff of the traversal just covered.

title: Depth-First Search

related.label: Depth-First Search: Recursive Traversal, Components, and Edge Classification

summary: Exploring a graph by plunging as deep as possible before backtracking — a different traversal order than BFS, naturally recursive, and the foundation for cycle detection and topological ordering.

title: Cycle Detection and Topological Sort

related.label: Topological Sort: Ordering a DAG via DFS Finish Times

summary: DFS timestamps reveal a cycle the instant one exists, and — when there isn't one — the same traversal produces a valid dependency order for every vertex in a directed acyclic graph.

title: Weighted Shortest Paths: Problem Setup
summary: Once edges carry weights, BFS's "fewest edges" answer stops being the same as "cheapest path" — the setup that motivates every shortest-path algorithm that follows.

title: Dijkstra's Algorithm

related.label: Heap Insert and Extract-Max/Min
Dijkstra's Algorithm: BFS Generalized to Weighted Graphs

summary: Always expanding the closest not-yet-finalized vertex next, using the binary heap already covered as its priority queue — correct whenever every edge weight is non-negative.

title: The Bellman-Ford Algorithm

related.label: Bellman-Ford: Shortest Paths with Negative Edges and Cycle Detection

summary: Dijkstra's algorithm breaks the instant an edge weight goes negative — Bellman-Ford trades speed for correctness in that case, and can even detect a negative-weight cycle that makes "shortest path" meaningless.

title: Shortest Paths in a DAG

related.label: Shortest Paths in a DAG: Topological Order Beats a Priority Queue

summary: When the graph is guaranteed acyclic, the topological order already covered lets shortest paths be computed in a single linear pass — no priority queue, no repeated relaxation, faster than either general algorithm.

title: Minimum Spanning Trees: Problem Framing

related.label: Minimum Spanning Trees: The Cut Property, Prim's, and Kruskal's

summary: Connecting every vertex of a weighted graph as cheaply as possible, using exactly the spanning-tree structure already covered in discrete math, now with a cost to minimize.

references.label: ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Algorithms and Complexity Knowledge Area

title: Kruskal's Algorithm

related.label: The Union-Find (Disjoint-Set) ADT

summary: Sort every edge by weight and add each one greedily, skipping any that would close a cycle — a connectivity check answered instantly by the union-find structure already covered.

title: Prim's Algorithm

related.label: Heap Insert and Extract-Max/Min

summary: A second, equally correct way to grow a minimum spanning tree — one vertex at a time from a single starting point, always adding the cheapest edge leaving the tree so far, using the same heap Dijkstra's algorithm relies on.

title: The Dynamic Programming Paradigm

related.label: Recursion
Dynamic Programming: Memoization, Tabulation, and Rod Cutting

summary: A problem qualifies for dynamic programming when it has overlapping subproblems (naive recursion redoes the same work over and over) and optimal substructure (an optimal solution is built from optimal solutions to its subproblems).

references.label: ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Algorithms and Complexity Knowledge Area

title: Memoization: Top-Down Dynamic Programming
summary: Take the exact naive recursive solution already familiar, cache each subproblem's answer the first time it's computed, and reuse it instead of recomputing — turning exponential time into polynomial with one small change.

title: Tabulation: Bottom-Up Dynamic Programming
summary: Instead of recursing downward and caching along the way, fill a table of subproblem answers starting from the smallest and building up — the same subproblems, computed in the opposite direction, with no recursion at all.

references.label: ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Algorithms and Complexity Knowledge Area

title: DP in Practice: Longest Common Subsequence

related.label: Longest Common Subsequence: The 2D DP Table

summary: Finding the longest sequence appearing (in order, not necessarily contiguously) in both of two strings — a two-dimensional table filled from a two-way recurrence, the canonical worked example of DP with more than one shrinking dimension.

title: DP in Practice: 0/1 Knapsack

related.label: 0-1 vs. Fractional Knapsack: Why the Same Structure Needs Different Techniques

summary: Choosing which items to pack, each either fully taken or fully left behind, to maximize value under a weight limit — the canonical worked example of DP where greedy provably fails and a full table is required.

references.label: ACM/IEEE CS2013 — Algorithms and Complexity Knowledge Area

title: DP in Practice: Longest Increasing Subsequence
summary: Finding the longest strictly increasing subsequence of a list — a one-dimensional DP whose naive O(n²) solution hides an O(n log n) speed-up built on the searching techniques already covered.

title: Choosing a Paradigm: A Decision Guide
summary: A closing, side-by-side guide across every paradigm covered — divide-and-conquer, greedy, and dynamic programming — organized by the tell-tale signs that point to each one, and worked through on problems that could plausibly go more than one way.
